title: Advanced Pipes and Cisterns — Leak Scenarios
tagline: Year 3 — Leaks, partial opening, timed valves and cisterns filling in stages

introduction.overview: Year 2 pipes and cisterns used inlets and outlets that stay open. Year 3 adds leaks that appear only after the tank has partly filled, pipes opened and closed at stated times, pipes that work in alternate hours, and capacity questions in litres. The rates still add, with outlets negative; the new difficulty is phases.
introduction.placementRelevance: Advanced pipe questions are commonly asked in company aptitude rounds, typically with a leak discovered after some time or pipes that open in turn.
introduction.realWorldContext: Filling reservoirs with seepage, bathtubs with a slow drain and chemical tanks with timed valves are of this type.

learningObjectives: Find the leak rate from filling times with and without the leak
Solve problems with phases of different open pipes
Handle pipes working in alternate hours
Compute capacity in litres from rates
Find the time to empty a partly full tank

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: Inlet rate = +1/time. Outlet or leak rate = −1/time. Net rate = sum. Work done = Σ rate × time.

coreDefinitions: Leak: an unintended outlet; its rate is the difference between the inlet rate and the net rate.
Phase: a period with a fixed set of open pipes.
Alternate hours: pipes open one at a time in turn, each for one hour.
Capacity: the volume the tank holds (the whole job = 1).
Net rate: the signed sum of the rates of open pipes.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: A tank is a job where outlets undo work. Filling a tank with a leak is like paying a tax: a fixed fraction of the inflow is lost every hour. Because rates add, a leak that appears midway simply changes the net rate from then on.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Write the rate of every pipe (units per hour using the LCM as capacity), list the phases with their open pipes and times, and add the units per phase until the capacity is reached.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Alternate hours
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Output per cycle = sum of the pipes

mainNarrative: To find a leak, compare the filling time with and without it. A pipe fills a tank in 6 hours; with a leak it takes 7.5 hours. The leak rate is 1/6 − 1/7.5 = 1/30, so the leak alone empties a full tank in 30 hours.

Phases: a tank is filled by a pipe (6 hours) for 3 hours, then a leak opens. After 3 hours the tank is half full. The net rate becomes 1/6 − 1/30 = 2/15, so the remaining half takes (1/2) ÷ (2/15) = 3.75 hours: 6.75 hours in all.

Alternate hours: if pipe A fills in 6 hours and pipe B in 8 hours and they work alternately (A first), the output per two hours is 1/6 + 1/8 = 7/24. After 6 cycles (12 hours) 42/24 would exceed the capacity, so use 3 cycles (6 hours, 21/24) and finish with A in the 7th hour: 1/6 = 4/24 ≥ 3/24 needed, so it takes just over 6.75 hours.
For litres, convert rates: a pipe that delivers 12 litres per minute and a leak that loses 2 litres per minute give a net 10 litres per minute, so a 600-litre tank fills in 60 minutes.
To empty a partly full tank, use the outlet rate only: with a leak of 1/30 per hour, half a tank empties in 15 hours.

deepDiveAspects.title: Leak is not constant in reality
deepDiveAspects.content: In the problems the leak rate is fixed; in practice leaks depend on water level. Treat them as constant unless told otherwise.

deepDiveAspects.title: Check with fractions
deepDiveAspects.content: Fractions of the tank filled in each phase must add to 1 at the end. Use this to check.

solvedExamples.title: Leak found
solvedExamples.question: A pipe fills a tank in 6 hours. Because of a leak it takes 7.5 hours. How long does the leak alone take to empty the tank?
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The leak removes what the inlet adds beyond the net.

solvedExamples.title: Leak after half-fill
solvedExamples.question: A pipe can fill a tank in 6 hours. After 3 hours a leak that empties a full tank in 30 hours appears. Find the total time to fill the tank.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The leak slows only the second half.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Applying the leak from the start.

solvedExamples.title: Capacity in litres
solvedExamples.question: An inlet delivers 12 litres per minute and a leak loses 2 litres per minute. How long does it take to fill a 600-litre tank?
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Rates in litres add like fractions.

traditionalVsShortcut.traditionalMethod: Recompute from scratch for every phase.
traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: List the pipes in each phase with their rates, find the net rate, and add the fraction filled in each phase.

commonMistakes.mistake: Applying the leak to the whole time
Forgetting the sign of an outlet

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: With a leak, the time must exceed the leak-free time.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Use the LCM capacity to avoid fractions.
